title: Molecular Shapes and Intermolecular Forces

cards.b: Water is a liquid but CO2 is a gas, though both are small molecules. Ice floats. A key fits one lock. Enzymes bind only the right molecule. All of this comes from molecular shape and the weak forces between molecules.

VSEPR (valence shell electron pair repulsion) says that electron pairs around a central atom spread as far apart as possible, like balloons tied together. The shape follows from counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.

• CO2: linear, 180°. Two bonding groups.
  • BF3: flat triangle, 120°.
  • CH4: tetrahedral, about 109.5°. Four bonds.
  • NH3: pyramidal, about 107°. Three bonds plus one lone pair.
  • H2O: bent, about 104.5°. Two bonds plus two lone pairs.

Lone pairs push harder than bonding pairs, squeezing the angles smaller.

A molecule is polar if its bond polarities do not cancel. CO2 has two polar C=O bonds, but they point opposite ways and cancel: non-polar. Water is bent, so its polarities add: polar.

Rule of thumb: like dissolves like. Polar solvents (water) dissolve polar or ionic substances; non-polar solvents (petrol) dissolve oils.

These are far weaker than bonds but control boiling point and state.

  • London dispersion forces: brief electron shifts create tiny dipoles. Present in all molecules, stronger with size. Explains why bigger alkanes are liquids.
  • Dipole-dipole: positive end of one polar molecule attracts negative end of another.
  • Hydrogen bond: a special strong dipole attraction when H is attached to N, O or F, and meets a lone pair on another N, O or F.

Hydrogen bonds give water a high boiling point (100 °C) compared with H2S (about -60 °C). Water is also densest at about 4 °C; as it freezes, hydrogen bonds lock molecules into an open lattice, so ice is less dense and floats. Lakes freeze from the top, letting fish survive below.

Hydrogen bonds also hold the two strands of DNA together and give proteins their folded shapes.

Shape of PH3: phosphorus has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair, like NH3. So pyramidal.

Shape of CCl4: four bonds, no lone pairs: tetrahedral, and non-polar since the bonds cancel.

Boiling order of CH4, H2O, HCl: CH4 (only weak dispersion, -162 °C) lowest; HCl (dipole-dipole, -85 °C) middle; H2O (hydrogen bonds, 100 °C) highest.

• Hydrogen bonds are not true bonds; they are attractions between molecules, about a tenth as strong as covalent bonds.
  • Boiling does not break covalent bonds. Boiling water leaves H2O molecules intact, only separated.
  • Having polar bonds does not make a molecule polar; shape matters.

G.N. Ramachandran (Madras, 1963) worked out which twist angles are allowed in protein chains, drawn as the Ramachandran plot, still used worldwide. He also helped decipher the triple-helix structure of collagen. His work shows that shape and hydrogen bonding decide how a protein folds.

• VSEPR: electron pairs spread out; lone pairs squeeze angles.
  • CH4 109.5, NH3 107, H2O 104.5, CO2 180.
  • Polarity depends on shape.
  • Dispersion, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonds set boiling points; hydrogen bonds make ice float.
